claims.text: TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, their SystemOne model, in the week before this post was published.
Jev is TypeSafe AI's SystemOne model.
TypeSafe's Jev comes with a set of AI primitives that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context.
Jev's decision-making primitives are confidence scoring, multiple choice, and yes/no (noul) questions.
In the past, having more infrastructure choices usually meant more complexity, which added technical debt.
GeoDeploy compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes, picks the best one for each geo, and provisions consistent environments across all three hyperscalers.
GeoDeploy's deployment request supports data-residency rules of EU-only, US-only, or in-country.
GeoDeploy's image input specifies platforms the container image is built for: amd64, arm64, or both.

In GeoDeploy, the TypeScript app takes in the request, fetches live pricing, and does all the math but makes no judgment calls; Jev decides which region wins and which modules to use but never does arithmetic, generates code, or invents region names; Pulumi provisions clusters, registries, workloads, and DNS but decides nothing.
GeoDeploy lists every region with managed Kubernetes and uses great-circle distance as a coverage measure.
GeoDeploy fetches current prices from the AWS Price List API, the Azure Retail Prices API, and the Google Cloud Billing Catalog, normalized into a single quote format.
GeoDeploy's deterministic TypeScript bin-packs pods onto nodes, filters out instance types that don't match the image's architecture, and computes a monthly cost for each candidate.
GeoDeploy composes a Pulumi program from a curated registry of typed modules: EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS through Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
GeoDeploy uses the Pulumi Automation API to run a preview and then an update, with one stack per region.
GeoDeploy won't provision unless cloud credentials pass readiness checks.
Every GeoDeploy run writes a plan.json and plan.md with the full decision record, and a web UI shows the deployment on a live globe.
The Pulumi Automation API page is at /automation/.
Jev doesn't return free text; it returns typed answers with calibrated confidence.
Jev's choice() primitive picks one option from a closed list and returns the pick, a probability distribution across all options, and a confidence.
Jev's score() primitive rates something against a rubric the user describes; GeoDeploy uses 10 levels.
Jev's noul() primitive answers a yes/no question with a single probability.
Because Jev only selects from closed sets and never writes code or does arithmetic, a hallucinated region like us-west-9 or made-up Pulumi argument can't happen by construction in GeoDeploy.
For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates, along with the constraints and the image's architecture, in a single call.

GeoDeploy asks Jev for one selection (choice), five quality scores (coverage, cost fit, maturity, sprawl risk, architecture consistency), two hard checks (noul: data residency and capacity), and a fallback region (choice).
GeoDeploy's question definitions live in packages/decide/src/questions.ts.
The TypeSafe SDK package @typesafe-ai/sdk exports choice, noul, and score functions.
TypeSafe's advice for writing rubrics is to "describe situations, not degrees."

GeoDeploy's rubrics use 10 levels, each a concrete scenario, running from "Serves users on a different continent with no nearby presence" to "In-geo with multiple availability zones, directly in or adjacent to the demand geo's primary population center."
The TypeSafeClient exposes a systemOne method taking state and questions and returning answers including selection.choice, selection.confidence, residencyOk.noul, and coverage.score.
GeoDeploy's ranking uses weight profiles: latency-optimized (default), balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain.
Because the weights live in code, GeoDeploy's ranking can be re-tuned without calling Jev again.

GeoDeploy's weight profiles are: latency-optimized {cost 0.13, coverage 0.48, maturity 0.17, sprawl 0.1, archConsistency 0.12}; balanced {0.25, 0.25, 0.2, 0.12, 0.18}; residency-first {0.12, 0.12, 0.38, 0.23, 0.15}; failure-domain {0.08, 0.17, 0.48, 0.15, 0.12}.
In GeoDeploy's composite score, sprawl risk is subtracted; every extra cloud provider means more credentials, tooling, and on-call runbooks.
In GeoDeploy, cluster and registry modules follow directly from the provider (AWS always means EKS and ECR), and Jev decides ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier.

GeoDeploy confidence thresholds: data residency 0.95 (hard reject); region for a new cluster 0.90 (top three candidates flagged for human choice); region when a stack already exists 0.75 (keep existing region); ingress or autoscaling module 0.85 (use registry default); node-pool sizing tier 0.60 (use bin-packing result); global floor for region pick, residency, or capacity 0.50 (drop the AI path for that geo).
The residency check is located in GeoDeploy's packages/decide/src/engine.ts.
Each AiPathAborted in GeoDeploy carries the full attempt (state, questions, and answers), so rejected answers end up in the audit trail.

If a gate check fails, the API times out or errors, or the upstream can't be reached, GeoDeploy switches to a deterministic fallback that compares prices across providers while still enforcing residency and constraint checks.
The `geodeploy explain` command shows why each region won.

GeoDeploy's `geodeploy monitor` command enables self-driving mode, in which the agent periodically checks each deployment's CPU utilization and asks Jev one joint question across all regions with options no-change, scale-up:<geo>, scale-down:<geo>, or shift:<from>-><to>, plus a separate check on disruption risk.
In GeoDeploy self-driving mode, code, not Jev, computes the actual node-count changes.

In GeoDeploy self-driving mode, above 0.85 confidence the resize is applied automatically; between 0.70 and 0.85 it is suggested for human approval; below 0.70 GeoDeploy ignores Jev's pick and falls back to a deterministic per-region rule based on observed utilization.
CPU utilization alone makes a poor autoscaling metric and is usually paired with other signals such as median end-to-end request latency and error rates once a traffic baseline is established.
GeoDeploy is released as open source at github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy, and getting started requires access to Jev and a cloud provider.
GeoDeploy places and scales Kubernetes across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud using Jev's confidence-scored decisions and the Pulumi Automation API.

GeoDeploy asks Jev to pick the best region per geo from a closed list, gates decisions on confidence with hard rejects for data residency, provisions consistent clusters with one Pulumi stack per region, and scales itself in self-driving mode with a human in the loop when confidence is low.
Pulumi's X account handle is @PulumiCorp.
